response.title: power station instead of a second battery for a camper van
response.answer:
Yes — a portable power station can replace a second (house) battery in a camper van, and for many camper van builds, it's actually the better choice.

Modern power stations from EcoFlow, BLUETTI, and Jackery combine a lithium battery, inverter, battery management system, and charging electronics in one unit.

The main question is whether you want a portable, plug-and-play setup or a permanently integrated van electrical system.

Power station vs. traditional house battery

Yes, with suitable charger

Repairability

	

More proprietary

	

Individual parts replaceable

Often higher

	

Often lower for larger systems




Best for

	

Weekend trips, simple builds

	

Full-time van life, custom systems

The biggest consideration: charging while driving

A traditional second battery is often charged by the vehicle's alternator through a DC-DC charger.

A portable power station can do the same, but the charging method matters enormously.

12V cigarette-lighter charging

Typically around 100–120W, depending on the vehicle and power station. A 1kWh battery can take roughly 10+ hours to recharge.

Slow

Dedicated alternator charger

Compatible systems can charge at several hundred watts or more. Some support approximately 800W, allowing a 1kWh power station to recharge in roughly 1.5 hours under favorable conditions.

Recommended

For a camper van, I would strongly favor a power station that supports a dedicated alternator charging solution, rather than relying on the cigarette-lighter socket.

Better for multi-day trips, a fridge, laptops and more demanding loads. Compatible with EcoFlow's alternator charging system. 
EcoFlow US
+1

One important limitation: many portable stations have only a 10A 12V output, which may not be sufficient for a complete van's DC distribution system. Also secure the station against movement, provide ventilation, and use properly fused wiring for any permanent connections.

My recommendation

For a camper van without a complex built-in electrical system, I'd lean toward a 2kWh LiFePO4 power station plus an alternator charger. It offers a useful balance of convenience, capacity and charging speed.

For a van with a permanently wired fridge, lights, water pump, diesel heater and other 12V appliances, a traditional LiFePO4 house battery system may be a better long-term solution.

One question: What do you plan to power in your camper van? For example, just a fridge, lights and phone charging, or also a diesel heater, microwave, induction cooktop or air conditioning?

That makes a big difference in whether a power station is a good replacement for a second battery.
